metadata.title: Surds and Simplifying Radicals
metadata.description: Recognize irrational roots, extract perfect powers, preserve the principal-root meaning, and check simplified forms exactly.
metadata.teachingApproach: Build rules from definitions, develop examples step by step, explain common misconceptions, and use exact checks. Each practice question has a targeted remedial explanation and a changed-value retry.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 9 “Surds and Indices,” printed pages 278–288. Approved scope: Define a surd as an irrational root expression and distinguish it from a radical that simplifies to a rational number. Teach square-root and cube-root simplification by factoring out the largest relevant perfect power, such as sqrt(72)=6sqrt(2) and cube-root(54)=3 cube-root(2). Explain the principal square root, nonnegative square-root convention, and why sqrt(x^2)=|x| for real x. Cover identifying equivalent forms, checking by squaring or cubing, and recognizing when no further simplification is possible. Use only the root orders and algebra level supported by Chapter 9; do not broaden into complex roots.

content.text: Welcome to Surds and Simplifying Radicals. We will build each rule from its meaning, work through exact examples, and use practice to check both the method and its conditions.

A radical is a symbol for a root; a surd is an irrational root expression. Some radicals are rational after simplification: sqrt(49)=7 is not a surd. sqrt(2) remains irrational and is a surd. The distinction is about the value, not merely whether a root sign appears.
The square-root symbol denotes the principal, nonnegative root. Thus sqrt(25)=5. The equation x^2=25 has two solutions, x=5 and x=−5, but the symbol sqrt(25) refers to 5 only.

To simplify a square root, factor the radicand into a perfect square times a leftover factor. Since sqrt(ab)=sqrt(a)sqrt(b) for nonnegative a,b, sqrt(72)=sqrt(36·2)=6sqrt(2). The factor outside the radical is the extracted square root.
Choose the largest perfect-square factor to reach simplest form in one step. For sqrt(180), use 180=36·5 and obtain 6sqrt(5). Using 4·45 is valid but leaves another square factor to extract.
The same idea works for cube roots using perfect cubes. Since 54=27·2, cube-root(54)=3 cube-root(2). For higher root orders, extract the largest factor whose exponent is a multiple of the root order.

Prime factorization makes the extraction systematic. For sqrt(2^5·3^2), pair two copies of each prime: one pair of 2s and the pair of 3s leave the root, while one 2 remains. The result is 2·3sqrt(2)=6sqrt(2).

A variable under a square root brings a sign issue. sqrt(x^2)=|x| because the principal square root cannot be negative. If the problem states x≥0, then |x|=x; without that condition, replacing it by x may be wrong.
For cube roots, cube-root(x^3)=x for every real x because the cube root preserves sign. Do not copy the absolute-value rule from square roots to odd roots.

A surd can be scaled without changing its value if the inside is adjusted by a square: 2sqrt(3)=sqrt(4·3)=sqrt(12). This can help compare forms, but the outside-coefficient form is usually simpler and easier to combine.
Example: simplify sqrt(48)+sqrt(75). Extract square factors separately: sqrt(48)=4sqrt(3) and sqrt(75)=5sqrt(3), so the sum is 9sqrt(3). The like radical appears only after simplification.
Example: simplify sqrt(12)·sqrt(6). Combine the nonnegative radicands to get sqrt(72), then simplify to 6sqrt(2). Alternatively, 2sqrt(3)·sqrt(6)=2sqrt(18)=6sqrt(2). Both paths agree.

Check a square-root simplification by squaring both sides. (6sqrt(2))^2=36·2=72, and both quantities are nonnegative, so sqrt(72)=6sqrt(2). Checking the square alone is not enough if the sign could differ; principal-root nonnegativity completes the argument.

Not every radical can be simplified to a rational number. If the prime exponents in a square-root radicand are not all even, some factor remains under the root. That leftover factor should contain no square divisor greater than 1.

Do not split a sum under a radical: sqrt(a+b) is generally not sqrt(a)+sqrt(b). For a=9,b=16, sqrt(25)=5, while 3+4=7. The product rule applies to multiplication of nonnegative radicands, not addition.

When comparing a radical with a rational number, first check signs, then square both nonnegative sides if useful. For instance, sqrt(7)>2 because both are nonnegative and 7>4. Squaring preserves order only in a domain where both sides are nonnegative.

A clean final form has no perfect-power factor left under the radical, no unnecessary coefficient inside, and any variable sign assumptions stated. These checks prevent a correct intermediate expression from becoming a misleading final answer.
Use the practice to identify which factor can leave the radical and how many copies remain. Then verify by reversing the operation: square a simplified square root or cube a simplified cube root.
